title: Learning Robot Learning
description: Sandbox for learning robot learning: a simulated car learns to drive to a goal through behavior cloning, DAgger, PPO, and residual RL.
summary: A step-by-step sandbox for learning the core methods of robot learning on one small task. A simulated unicycle car with noisy sensors has to turn around and drive to a random goal about 3 m away. It builds up from a neural network written by hand in NumPy, through behavior cloning and DAgger, to PPO. The final stage is residual RL, where PPO may only nudge a frozen behavior-cloned policy within a hard-bounded window.
what_i_did: Wrote an MLP from scratch in NumPy (forward pass, backprop, SGD) and used it to clone a demonstrator, then fixed compounding error with DAgger.
Built the unicycle environment and a Gymnasium wrapper, plus three demonstrators: a smooth P-controller, a 'turn then drive' policy, and an 'x then y' policy that mimics human driving styles.
Trained a Stable-Baselines3 PPO baseline from scratch with no demonstrations.
Trained a PyTorch behavior cloning policy on 50 human-style demos, using a trajectory-level train/val split and a network that rewrites observations into the car's body frame.

Implemented residual PPO, a = μ_BC(obs) + [dv, dω] ⊙ a_PPO, with the bound enforced as a hard clip instead of a reward penalty, and swept the speed bound dv to measure how far the policy drifts from the demonstrator as the constraint loosens.

title: Lunar Rock Collection Robot
description: RoboHacks (YC Hackathon) Project: an autonomous robot that identifies, collects, and sorts rocks built with Innate's MARS Robot.
summary: Luna is a rock-collection rover built in a weekend at YC RoboHacks (~10% acceptance) on top of Innate's MARS robot. The robot drives over a simulated lunar surface, spots rocks with a vision-language model and object detection pipeline, picks them up with a modified gripper, and drops them into onboard sorting bins. The picking motion itself is a learned policy rather than a scripted trajectory, trained from teleoperation demonstrations and exposed as a skill the robot's VLM agent can call.
what_i_did: Prototyped the hardware additions: grippers sized for the rock samples, sorting bins mounted on the chassis, and a force-sensitive resistor (FSR) embedded in the gripper.
Collected ~50 teleoperation demonstrations of rock picking and trained an ACT (Action Chunking Transformer) policy on them.
Deployed the trained policy as a skill for the robot's VLM agent, so the high-level planner decides what to pick and the learned policy handles how.
results: Demo: the rover finds, picks, and sorts rocks autonomously on the sandbox surface.

title: Pan-Tilt-Zoom Tracking Camera
description: PTZ camera with realtime object detection and tracking.
summary: A camera that finds an object with YOLO and physically turns to keep it centered. A webcam sits on 3D printed mounts driven by a stepper motor for pan and a servo for tilt, both controlled by an Arduino, with a laptop running detection and control.
what_i_did: Built the vision pipeline in Python with OpenCV and YOLO, smoothing the detected target position to avoid jitter.
Designed the control logic: velocity control for the pan stepper and eased position control for the tilt servo, so motion stays smooth despite a discrete command stream.
Added firmware safety interlocks: a watchdog that stops motion if commands drop out, plus hard limits on both axes.
Implemented automatic digital zoom that keeps the subject at a constant apparent size, with a deadband so the crop doesn't breathe on a still target.
Designed and 3D printed the mounts in Onshape, built the motor and Arduino circuit, and calibrated the axes before closing the loop.
future_steps: Depth-based zoom using a monocular depth model, so framing follows actual distance rather than bounding box size.
A self-contained build on a PCB with enclosed wiring and aligned mounts.
Natural language control for picking the subject and composing the shot.

title: E-Throttle
description: Electronic Throttle Controller for Full Blue Racing (University of Cambridge's Formula Student Team).
summary:
The electronic throttle (E-Throttle) project replaces the mechanical throttle cable with an electronically controlled throttle body, which brings benefits such as improved control of the fuel/air ratio. The goal is to redesign and validate the Electronic Throttle Control for proper operation and compliance with Formula Student safety regulations.

The E-Throttle system consists of two Accelerator Pedal Position Sensors (APPS) at the pedal, two Throttle Position Sensors (TPS) with a stepper motor at the throttle body, and a central control board. This controller processes sensor inputs and implements redundant, safety-critical control in compliance with the Formula Student regulations.
what_i_did: Breadboard prototyped open-loop control of the stepper motor from the APPS sensors before committing to a board design.

Designed the control PCB in KiCad with hardware-level safety built in: independent watchdog timers, high-side FETs, and relays, so a firmware hang or sensor fault cuts power to the throttle actuator without relying on the microcontroller.
Assembled the board and tested each subsystem individually (power, sensor inputs, watchdog, FET and relay switching, stepper driver). All components functional.
Developing the throttle controller firmware on the ESP32 to drive the stepper motor from APPS input with closed-loop feedback from the TPS sensors.
future_steps: Closed-loop PID control of throttle position using TPS feedback.
Software safety features required by the regulations: plausibility checks between the redundant APPS and TPS sensors, and safe shutdown on implausible readings.
Integrate with the car and validate the full system against the Formula Student safety rules.

title: Mobile Manipulator Simulation
description: ROS2 robot that maps an environment, navigates it autonomously, and detects what is in it — simulated in Gazebo.
summary: A simulated robot that maps an unknown space, navigates it autonomously, and is being extended to recognise what is in it. A TurtleBot3 runs in Gazebo on ROS2, mapping with slam_toolbox, navigating with Nav2, and carrying a custom depth camera that feeds a YOLO detector node.
what_i_did: Built the simulation bringup as a self-contained ROS2 package so one launch argument selects the robot model, URDF, and topic bridge together; tuned sensor rates to run near real time.
Brought up SLAM with slam_toolbox and mapped both a stock world and a custom house world using a waypoint tour node driven by the SLAM-corrected pose.
Implemented autonomous navigation with Nav2 and AMCL against a saved map, verified with a scripted goal test instead of clicking in RViz.
Extended the stock robot into an RGBD model and cross-checked the depth against LiDAR so detections can later be projected into 3D.
Wrote a YOLO detector node that publishes standard vision_msgs detections, dropping frames rather than queueing them to keep latency bounded.
future_steps: Fuse depth with LiDAR to lift 2D detections into 3D on the map, so objects are remembered by location.
Filter dynamic objects like people out of the static map while still avoiding them locally.
Frontier exploration with Nav2 so the robot maps rooms beyond the one it starts in.
Add the WidowX 250 arm and drive pick-and-place with MoveIt2 from the semantic map.
LLM task planner that turns a natural language instruction into navigation goals and grasps.

title: Infrared Imaging Drone
description: Quadcopter drone with downward-facing infrared camera for birds-eye thermal imaging.
summary: A self-built quadcopter carrying a downward-facing FLIR Lepton thermal camera, intended for birds-eye thermal imaging of the ground below. The airframe is built around a Pixhawk 2.4.8 flight controller with GPS, four ESC-driven motors, a power distribution board, and an RC receiver, and can fly either under manual radio control or autonomously along a Mission Planner route. A Raspberry Pi 4B mounted on the frame runs the thermal camera.
what_i_did: Assembled the quadcopter frame and soldered the electronics: Pixhawk flight controller, GPS, four ESCs and motors, power distribution board, LiPo battery, buzzer, safety switch, and RC receiver.
Calibrated the Pixhawk (accelerometer, compass, radio, ESCs) and set up autonomous missions in Mission Planner.
Designed a camera holder in Onshape to mount the FLIR Lepton and Raspberry Pi under the frame, facing downward.
Set up the thermal imaging pipeline on the Raspberry Pi using LeptonModule to drive the FLIR Lepton, with a Qt GUI for viewing and capturing images.
results: Drone flies manually with the remote control or autonomously along a Mission Planner waypoint route.
Thermal camera captures clear infrared images (e.g. grass vs. brick boundary), but capture is still triggered manually rather than automatically in flight.

title: Roller Coaster Modeling and Simulation
description: CAD design a roller coaster and simulate its movement along a track.
summary: A roller coaster designed and simulated entirely in SolidWorks. The cart and track were modelled as separate parts and combined into an assembly, then run through SolidWorks physics-based motion simulation to check that the ride stays within safe speed and acceleration limits along the whole track.
what_i_did: Used SolidWorks to design a roller coaster assembly, including cart and track.
Ran physics simulations in SolidWorks to analyze the motion of the cart along the track, extracting speed and lateral/vertical acceleration profiles.
results: Top speed of roughly 30 mph along the track.
Maximum lateral acceleration of about 0.4 g and maximum vertical acceleration of about 1.7 g, within typical rider-safety limits.

title: LED Magnetometer
description: Analog signal-conditioning circuit that displays magnetic field strength on a 4-level LED bar.
summary: A fully analog magnetometer readout. The raw sensor output is small and sits on a DC offset, so it is first passed through a cascaded op-amp stage that removes the offset and amplifies the signal into a usable range. The conditioned signal then drives a bank of comparators with staggered thresholds, lighting one to four LEDs as the field strength increases. No microcontroller is involved.
what_i_did: Designed and built a cascaded op-amp circuit to amplify and remove the offset from the magnetometer signal.
Designed and built a multi-threshold comparator circuit to drive the 4-level LED display.
Prototyped on breadboard and verified each stage with an oscilloscope.
results: LED bar responds proportionally to field strength as a magnet is brought closer (see video).
